en: An acorn glows in Gail’s familiar room.
Its golden light opens a doorway into a woodland clearing.
Gail meets a little elf named Nori beside his tree house.
He is worried about growing up and having new things to learn.
A young bird rests on a low branch near the house.
Nori watches its small wings and wishes it could stay just as it is.
Nori shows Gail his old tree house, where everything feels familiar.
He worries that growing up might mean losing the things he loves.
Nori tells Gail that change makes him nervous.
He wonders if stopping the forest will keep everything safe and familiar.
Nori uses the acorn to hold the clearing in a frozen moment.
Nothing is icy or cold, but the plants and animals can no longer change.
Gail points to a pink bud beside the path.
Nori had wanted to see its petals, but the frozen moment keeps it closed.
The green apple is still unripe and needs more time on the tree.
With the clearing held still, it cannot become the red apple Nori was waiting for.
The young bird needs time for its wings to grow stronger.
Nori begins to see that staying the same also keeps new possibilities out of reach.
Gail explains that growing up does not mean knowing everything at once.
Nori can learn a little at a time and ask someone to help.
Gail asks Nori to imagine how the woods change from one season to the next.
Different parts of the year bring different things to notice.
Nori imagines the woodland in spring, with small buds beginning to open.
If every moment stayed the same, he would miss these little beginnings.
Next, Nori imagines summer, with warm days and leafy places to sit.
He remembers things he enjoys about this different part of the year.
Nori imagines autumn and the orange leaves along the path.
The woods would look different, yet his familiar tree house could still be there.
Nori imagines the quiet woods in winter, with a little snow on the path.
Change can include a time to rest, as well as a time to begin.
Gail reminds Nori that the winter snow he imagined will melt when warmer days return.
The end of one season can make room for the next.
Nori decides to allow change and releases the acorn’s spell.
The woodland moves again; as time passes, the bud opens into a pink bloom.
More days pass in the changing woodland, and the apple becomes red and ripe.
Nori is glad that he allowed the tree the time it needed.
With time and practice, the bird grows stronger and tries a new flight.
Nori is still learning too, beside the same old tree house and a friend who helps.
The acorn’s light brings Gail back to her familiar room.
She remembers that she can welcome something new without giving up everything she loves.
